title: Gandhian Nationalism (1927–1937)
tagline: The Simon Commission, the Nehru Report, civil disobedience, the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, the Round Table Conferences and the Government of India Act of 1935.

overview.intro: The years between 1927 and 1937 carried Indian nationalism from a constitutional confrontation to mass civil disobedience and then to a partial transfer of power. This unit covers the all-White Simon Commission and the Indian response, the Nehru Report as the first dominion-status constitution produced by Indians, the Civil Disobedience Movement with the Salt March and the Lahore session, the Gandhi–Irwin Pact and the Round Table Conferences, and finally the Government of India Act of 1935 with the elections of 1937 and the formation of ministries.

learn.title: The Simon Commission and the Nehru Report

blocks.text: The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927 to review the working of the constitutional reforms of 1919 and reported in 1930. It contained no Indian member, and its arrival at Bombay in 1928 was met with a total hartal, processions and the slogan Simon Go Back. The all-White composition convinced Indians that the future of their country was to be decided without them. The demonstration against the commission in Lahore on 30 October 1928 included a police lathi charge in which Lala Lajpat Rai was injured, and he died a few weeks later, an event that entered nationalist memory as a sacrifice demanding an answer.

In response, an All Parties Conference met in 1928 and appointed a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru to prepare a constitution for India. The Nehru Report proposed dominion status, a federal structure with residuary powers in the centre, a bicameral legislature, and universal adult franchise in principle, while rejecting separate electorates in favour of reserved seats with adult suffrage. Subhas Chandra Bose moved that it should accept complete independence, and when the motion was lost he and some associates withdrew from the committee. The failure of the British to accept dominion status at the Round Table Conferences pushed the Congress at the Lahore session of December 1929 to adopt purna swaraj as its goal, and 26 January 1930 was observed as the first Independence Day.

learn.title: Civil disobedience and the Salt March

blocks.text: Gandhi presented eleven demands to the Viceroy in January 1930, of which the most accessible was the reduction of the salt tax, since salt was a necessity used by every household and taxed by the state on its manufacture. Receiving no satisfactory reply, he set out from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with seventy-eight followers on the Dandi March, walking some 240 miles over twenty-four days and picking up a lump of natural salt from the shore on 6 April. The act was deliberately chosen: breaking a salt law was trivially simple to copy, it affected the poorest person as much as the richest, and it made the law itself look absurd.

The response was immediate and wider than any previous movement. Salt was made and sold illegally across the country, foreign cloth was boycotted, forest laws were defied by tribals, and revenue non-payment was attempted in several districts. The government replied with mass arrests, including Gandhi’s own on 5 May 1930, the closure of the Congress and the press, and force in the cities. The movement continued underground and resumed in 1931, and it demonstrated that a single symbolic act could mobilise an entire country.

learn.title: The Gandhi–Irwin Pact and the Round Table Conferences

blocks.text: The first Round Table Conference met in London in 1930 with the Congress absent, since its members were in jail, and it therefore achieved little on the constitutional question. The Gandhi–Irwin Pact of March 1931 ended the first phase of civil disobedience: the government released most political prisoners, permitted the making of salt for personal use, and restored confiscated property, while Gandhi agreed to attend the second Round Table Conference as the Congress representative. The conference itself broke down over the communal question, with the Muslim League and other parties insisting on safeguards and separate representation that the Congress delegation would not accept in the form proposed.

blocks.text: Gandhi returned to India to find the movement’s position changed, and the renewed campaign of early 1932 was met with sterner repression. The movement wound down by 1934 without the political objective being achieved, but it had demonstrated mass participation on an unprecedented scale and had kept the constitutional question open for the negotiations that produced the Act of 1935.

learn.title: The Government of India Act of 1935 and the ministries of 1937

blocks.text: The Government of India Act of 1935, drawn from the White Paper published after the third conference, introduced an All-India Federation of the provinces and the princely states, provincial autonomy with responsible government in the provinces, a federal legislature with a lower and upper house, and the right of Indians to hold office. It retained strong safeguards for the governor-general and the services, and it granted separate electorates with weighted representation for minorities, which the Congress had opposed. Its franchise expanded to about a fourth of the adult population, which was a large increase though far from universal.

The elections of 1936–37 were held under the Act, and the Congress won a clear majority of the seats it contested, forming ministries in eight provinces between 1937 and 1939. In office the Congress ministries carried out much of their programme in education, agrarian relief and public health, and resigned in 1939 when the viceroy declared India a belligerent in the Second World War without consulting Indian leaders. The tenures showed that Indians could govern a province, and the resignation turned the provincial question into a further argument about the authority of the colonial state.

questions.prompt: The demand for complete independence adopted at the Lahore session of 1929 is called purna __________ .
questions.explanation: Its adoption led to 26 January 1930 being observed as the first Independence Day.

questions.prompt: The agreement of March 1931 between Gandhi and the Viceroy that ended the first phase of civil disobedience is the Gandhi– __________ Pact.
questions.explanation: The pact secured the release of political prisoners and permission to make salt for personal use in exchange for the Congress attending the second Round Table Conference.

questions.prompt: State four reasons why salt was chosen as the issue for civil disobedience.
questions.answer: Four reasons are: it was used by every household, rich and poor, so the issue was universal; the tax fell heaviest on the poorest, making the injustice easy to demonstrate; breaking the law required no organisation, no money and no special skill, so anyone could copy it; and salt manufacture was a state monopoly, so the confrontation was directly with the government. Its visibility in everyday life is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each reason must connect the choice of issue to the capacity for mass participation.

questions.prompt: Describe the main provisions of the Government of India Act of 1935.
questions.answer: The Act proposed an All-India Federation of the provinces and the princely states, though the states never joined. It granted provincial autonomy, with each province having a governor and a legislature responsible for the provincial services, which was the most substantial concession. It provided for a federal legislature with two houses at the centre while retaining strong safeguards for the governor-general and the services. It widened the electorate substantially, though only to about a quarter of the adult population, and it retained separate electorates with weighted representation for minorities, which the Congress had opposed. Reserved seats and safeguards preserved decisive authority with the British.
questions.explanation: Four provisions are required, and the distinction between what was granted and what was retained earns the remaining marks.

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of the Round Table Conferences and the Gandhi–Irwin Pact.
questions.answer: The Round Table Conferences were significant because they were the first formal discussions of India’s constitutional future with Indian participants, though the Congress was absent from the first and third. The first conference of 1930 met while the Congress leadership was in jail, so it could not represent the largest Indian party and produced little agreement. The Gandhi–Irwin Pact of March 1931 ended the first phase of civil disobedience: the government released most political prisoners, permitted salt to be made for personal use and restored confiscated property, while Gandhi agreed to attend the second conference as the Congress representative. That conference failed because the communal question could not be settled, with the League and other parties demanding safeguards and separate representation that the Congress would not accept in the proposed form. The third conference proceeded without the Congress and produced the White Paper on which the Act of 1935 was based. The significance is therefore double: the conferences established that the constitutional question had to be negotiated with Indian parties, and their failure over the communal issue left a legacy of mistrust that shaped the politics of the following decade.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sequence, the terms of the pact and a judgement on what the conferences did and did not resolve.

questions.prompt: Assess the claim that the Government of India Act of 1935 was a real transfer of power rather than a limited reform.
questions.answer: The argument for a real transfer rests on the substance of provincial autonomy. Elected ministers were responsible to the provincial legislatures for a wide field of administration including education, agriculture, health and public works, and the Congress, having won a majority of the seats it contested, governed eight provinces from 1937 to 1939. The franchise expanded to about a quarter of the adult population, Indians held office at the centre, and the legislature had control over a larger part of the budget than before. The argument for a limited reform is equally concrete: the governor-general retained reserve powers, the services and the armed forces stayed under British control, the federation of princely states never came into existence, separate electorates and weighted representation continued to shape the electorate, and India was declared a belligerent in 1939 without any consultation, which showed that the ultimate authority had not moved. The most accurate judgement is that the Act transferred responsibility for provincial administration while reserving power over defence, foreign affairs and the constitution itself, and that the resignation of the Congress ministries in 1939 demonstrated both the reality of the transferred power and the limits placed on it.
questions.explanation: Marks are for weighing specific provisions on both sides and reaching a reasoned judgement rather than accepting either label.
